messages.subject: Silent reject statement
parts:
I am building a model using a generalized extreme value distribution, a 3 parameters distribution, which has support that depends on the parameters. Because I cannot do vector constraints on the parameters, I need to resort to using a reject statement for combinations of parameters that don't work. 

My model is working fine and converging to reasonable values but I get an "Informational Message" from my own reject statement nearly every iteration. 

My request is to have a "silent_reject()" function so that I don't get thousands of lines of the same message. 


Thanks,
Cameron

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Silent reject statement
parts:
I am fitting hundreds of GEV distributions in spatial setting so all the GEV parameters (location, scale and shape) are vectors. The constraint is that 1 + (y - loc) * shape / scale > 0, for all y. Setting these constraints in a univariate case is strait forward, but every element of the parameter vectors needs a different constraint.

The full model is very dense but I can send that to if it would help. The code for the log probability where I use the reject is below.

Thanks,
Cameron

real gev_v_log (vector y, real loc, real scale, real shape){
    real inv_shape;
    real inv_shape_p1;
    real neg_inv_shape;
    vector[rows(y)] z;
    vector[rows(y)+1] lp;
    int N;

    N <- rows(y);

    inv_shape <- 1.0/shape;
    inv_shape_p1 <- inv_shape + 1;
    neg_inv_shape <- -inv_shape;

    z <- 1 + (y - loc) * shape / scale;

    for(n in 1:N){
      # because we cannot do vector constraints
      if(z[n] < 0.0){
        reject("Invalid GEV parameters");
      }

      lp[n] <-  inv_shape_p1*log(z[n]) + pow(z[n],neg_inv_shape);
    }
    lp[N+1] <- log(scale) * N;
    return -sum(lp);  
  }

    vector<lower=0>[rows(y)] z;

Daniel

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Silent reject statement
parts:
On Wednesday, March 11, 2015 at 11:10:44 AM UTC-4, Cameron Bracken wrote:

I am fitting hundreds of GEV distributions in spatial setting so all the GEV parameters (location, scale and shape) are vectors. The constraint is that 1 + (y - loc) * shape / scale > 0, for all y. Setting these constraints in a univariate case is strait forward, but every element of the parameter vectors needs a different constraint.

Does the following work for you? The idea is to decompose the scale parameter into a unit_scale parameter and a multiple thereof. Given y, loc, shape and unit_scale, you can figure out what multiple has to be such that (y - loc) * shape / (multiple * unit_scale) > -1 for all observations.

parameters {
  vector[N] loc;
  vector[N] shape;
  vector<lower=0>[N] unit_scale;
  real<lower=abs(min(0,min((y - loc) * shape ./ unit_scale)))> multiple;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[N] scale;
  scale <- unit_scale * multiple;
}

Ben

messages.author: 115bcf2cc8b220a2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Silent reject statement
parts:
Thanks for the suggestions, I think your approach would work Ben, except that in my model, the GEV parameters are latent and get computed on the fly. Taking out the reject statement works, but there is no guarantee that valid values are being sampled. My model is below. 

Thanks, Cameron

functions {

  real gev_log (real y, real loc, real scale, real shape){
    vector<lower=0>[1] z;
    real inv_shape; 

    inv_shape <- 1.0/shape;

    z[1] <- 1 + (y - loc) * shape / scale;
    #if(z[1] < 0.0){
    #    reject("Invalid GEV parameters");
    #}

    return -log(scale) - (1 + inv_shape)*log(z[1]) - pow(z[1],-inv_shape);  
  }

  matrix exp_cov_matrix (matrix x, real partial_sill, real range, real nugget){

    int S;
    matrix[dims(x)[1],dims(x)[1]] cov;

    S <- dims(x)[1];

    // off-diagonal elements
    for (i in 1:(S-1)) {
      for (j in (i+1):S) {
        # beta0 = partial_sill = scale^2
        # beta1 = range = phi
        cov[i,j] <- partial_sill * exp(-1.0/range * x[i,j]);
        cov[j,i] <- cov[i,j];
      }
    }

    // diagonal elements
    for (k in 1:S)
      cov[k,k] <- partial_sill + nugget;

    return cov;

  }

}

data {
  int<lower=1> S; // number of locations
  int<lower=1> T; // number of time data points
  int<lower=1> PS; // number of space predictors
  int<lower=1> PT; // number of time predictors
  matrix[T,S] y; // observations
  matrix[S,PS] space_covariates; // such as elevation
  matrix[T,PT] time_covariates; // such as enso
  matrix[S,S] dist; //distance matrix

  vector<lower=0>[2] cov_pars_loc_init;
  vector<lower=0>[2] cov_pars_scale_init;

  // include an intercept
  vector[PS+1] beta_space_loc_init;
  vector[PS+1] beta_space_scale_init;

  // the first predictor is always time (linear trend)
  vector[PT+1] beta_time_loc_init;
  vector[PT+1] beta_time_scale_init;

}

transformed data {
  matrix[S, PS+1] X_s;
  matrix[T, PT+1] X_t;

  real min_y;
  real max_y;
  real mean_y;
  real max_dist;

  vector[S] zero_vector;

  for (s in 1:S) 
    zero_vector[s] <- 0;

  // fill the space predictor matrix 
  for(i in 1:S)
    for(j in 1:PS)
      X_s[i,j+1] <- space_covariates[i,j];

  // intercept 
  for(i in 1:S)
      X_s[i,1] <- 1;

  // fill the time predictor matrix 
  for(i in 1:T)
    for(j in 1:PT)
      X_t[i,j+1] <- time_covariates[i,j];

  // time trend 
  for(i in 1:T)
      X_t[i,1] <- i;

  min_y <- min(y);
  max_y <- max(y);
  mean_y <- mean(y);
  max_dist <- max(dist);

}

parameters {
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> shape[T];                 // shape 

  vector<lower=0, upper=max_dist>[2] cov_pars_loc;
  vector<lower=0, upper=max_dist>[2] cov_pars_scale;

  // regression coefficients
  vector[PS+1] beta_space_loc;
  vector[PS+1] beta_space_scale;

  vector[PT+1] beta_time_loc;
  vector[PT+1] beta_time_scale;

  vector[S] resid_loc[T]; // location
  vector[S] resid_scale[T];     // scale 

} 

model {    

    matrix[S,S] L_loc;
    matrix[S,S] L_scale;

    vector[S] loc[T]; // location
    vector[S] scale[T];     // scale 

    // priors on space parameters
    cov_pars_loc[1] ~ normal(cov_pars_loc_init[1],100);
    //cov_pars_loc[2] ~ uniform(0,max_dist);
    cov_pars_scale[1] ~ normal(cov_pars_scale_init[1],100);
    //cov_pars_scale[2] ~ uniform(0,max_dist);

    // regression coefficients (weakly informative priors)
    beta_space_loc ~ normal(beta_space_loc_init, 100);
    beta_space_scale ~ normal(beta_space_scale_init, 100);
    beta_time_loc ~ normal(beta_time_loc_init, 100);
    beta_time_scale ~ normal(beta_time_scale_init, 100);

    // compute covariance matricies on the fly
    // Use the cholesky decomposition to avoid inverting the matrix each time step
    L_loc <- cholesky_decompose(exp_cov_matrix(dist, cov_pars_loc[1], cov_pars_loc[2], 0.0));
    L_scale <- cholesky_decompose(exp_cov_matrix(dist, cov_pars_scale[1], cov_pars_scale[2], 0.0));

    // gaussian process on the gev parameters
    // µ = X_t*ß_t + X_s*ß_s + e ; e ~ MVN(0,∑)
    for(t in 1:T){
      resid_loc[t] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zero_vector, L_loc);
      resid_scale[t] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zero_vector, L_scale);

      for(s in 1:S){
        loc[t,s] <- row(X_s,s) * beta_space_loc + row(X_t,t) * beta_time_loc + resid_loc[t,s];
        scale[t,s] <- row(X_s,s) * beta_space_scale + row(X_t,t) * beta_time_scale + resid_scale[t,s];

        # log probability for the marginals 
        y[t,s] ~ gev(loc[t,s], scale[t,s], shape[t]);
      }

    }

}

in functions (or anywhere else).  They will not be tested or
respected.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Silent reject statement
parts:
On Wednesday, March 11, 2015 at 11:01:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'm not sure about the extent of the Jacobian warnings.  It's
a huge pain and it's another case where I wonder if the false positives
are worth it.  On the other hand, users really shouldn't be using
transforms they don't understand, although many are harmless (i.e.,
don't require Jacobian corrections).

I misread Cameron's code, and it seems the parser would catch the need for a Jacobian if one were needed even if utilizing user-defined sampling statements. I guess I would just tweak the warning from

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) contains a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
 You must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
...

to

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may entail a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
 If so, you must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform in order to draw from the posterior distribution of the parameters. See the chapter in the Stan User Manual on "Transformations of Variables".

Ben
